Red, Itchy or Weepy?

Pink Eye and Conjunctivitis: Answers for Pine Beach Families

Book AppointmentCall: (732) 978-9306

Pink eye tends to show up overnight. You go to bed feeling fine and wake to a red, gritty eye and lashes glued together—or your child does, on a school morning. Waking up to pink eye can feel alarming, but it doesn’t have to be. It’s common and usually mild, and knowing which kind you’re dealing with makes the next step much clearer.

What Pink Eye Is

Pink eye is the everyday name for conjunctivitis, an inflammation of the thin, clear layer that covers the white of the eye and lines the inside of the eyelids. Viruses cause most cases in adults, and bacteria cause many in children. Allergies and irritants such as smoke and pool chlorine can bring it on too. You might notice:

  • A pink or red tint to the white of the eye
  • Watering, or a discharge that may be clear, white, yellow or green
  • Itching, burning or a sandy feeling
  • Crusty lashes or lids that stick together in the morning
  • Puffy eyelids

Why the Cause Makes a Difference

  • Different kinds need different care. Viral pink eye usually runs its course, bacterial pink eye may call for prescription drops, and allergic pink eye is handled another way entirely.
  • Other problems can look the same. A scratch on the eye, a trapped particle, a contact lens problem or inflammation inside the eye can all cause redness, and some of these need prompt treatment.
  • A clear plan helps the whole household. Knowing the cause tells you how to ease the discomfort, how to stop it spreading and when to go back to school or work.

What an Eye Visit for Pink Eye Usually Involves

When an eye doctor checks a red, weepy eye, the visit usually includes:

  1. Questions about when it started, which eye is affected and whether anyone around you has had it
  2. A quick check of how well each eye sees
  3. A magnified look at the white of the eye, the clear front surface and the inside of the eyelids
  4. A plain-language talk about the likely cause, what will help and what to watch for

Why Store-Bought Drops or Waiting It Out Can Fall Short

Redness-relief drops from the pharmacy can make an eye look whiter for a few hours, but they don’t treat what’s causing the redness, and frequent use can leave eyes redder. Antibiotic drops won’t help a virus, and leftover drops from an old prescription—or someone else’s—aren’t a safe bet. Waiting is reasonable for a mild case that’s already improving, but the kinds are hard to tell apart at home.

When to Get Help Promptly

Call an eye doctor promptly if you notice:

  • Eye pain, not just mild irritation
  • Sensitivity to light
  • Blurry vision that doesn’t clear when you blink
  • Redness in a contact lens wearer
  • Symptoms that get worse, or don’t start to improve after a few days
  • Pink eye in someone with a weakened immune system

For a newborn with red or sticky eyes, call your baby’s doctor right away.

Go to the nearest emergency room right away for sudden vision loss, a chemical splash, an injury that cuts or punctures the eye, a curtain or shadow over part of your vision, or flashes of light with a sudden shower of new floaters. None of these is typical of pink eye, and none should wait.

A Familiar Office Close to Home

Academy Vision has been part of this community for decades, and our team is made up of experienced optometrists who take the time to listen, explain and make sure you feel comfortable. When redness or discomfort won’t go away, we offer emergency eye care in Pine Beach whenever possible. Medical insurance comes into play for health-related concerns such as eye infections, and our team can help you understand your benefits.

For other urgent problems, see our pages on red, irritated eyes, something stuck in your eye and emergency eye care.

Is pink eye contagious?

Viral and bacterial pink eye spread easily through hands, towels and pillowcases; allergic pink eye doesn’t spread. At home, wash hands often, keep hands away from your eyes, use your own towel, change pillowcases often and don’t share eye makeup. Contact lens wearers should leave lenses out until the eyes are back to normal, then start fresh with new lenses and a new case.

Should my child stay home from school or daycare?

It depends on the cause and on the school’s rules, since many schools and daycares set their own policies. Allergic pink eye isn’t contagious. For the viral or bacterial kind, check with the school nurse and ask your child’s doctor when it’s reasonable to go back. The same goes for adults who work closely with others.

How soon should pink eye be checked?

Right away for any of the warning signs above. For a mild case, call if it isn’t improving after a few days or gets worse at any point. Questions in the meantime? Call us at (732) 978-9306 to ask.

We’re Right Here When You Need Us

Our Services at Academy Vision

  • Emergency Eye Care »

    Eyes don’t pick convenient moments to act up. A branch catches you while you’re trimming the hedges, one eye turns red and sore overnight, or a blur shows up that wasn’t there yesterday.

  • Red Eye Treatment »

    A red eye can be a small annoyance or a sign that something needs attention soon.

  • Dry Eye Treatment »

    If your eyes feel irritated, tired, or constantly dry, we’ll find the cause and help you get real relief.

  • Foreign Body Removal »

    A grain of sand on a breezy day at the shore, sawdust from a weekend project, a stray eyelash—it doesn’t take much to make an eye sting, water and feel like something’s caught in it.

  • Flashes & Floaters »

    Maybe it’s a cobweb that drifts across the page while you read, or a quick flicker at the corner of your eye when you turn your head in a dim room.
